e.etymology: A short form of Adolphus, the Latin form of Germanic Adolf, from adal, noble, and wolf.
A pet form or respelling of Hosea, the Old Testament prophet, whose Hebrew name Hoshea means salvation.
An American compound of the early 1900s that joins Willo, from Willa or Willow, with Dean.
Old English ecg, the edge of a sword, plus beorht, bright. Egbert of Wessex was a 9th-century king, grandfather of Alfred the Great, and the name was revived in the 19th century.
A spelling of Freddie, the pet form of Frederick, from Germanic frid, peace, and ric, ruler. It also served for Alfred and for girls named Frederica or Winifred.
An English surname taken from places called Marland, used now and then as a given name in the early 20th century.
Usually taken as a short form of Clellan or Cleland, Scottish surnames used as given names in 19th-century America.
A spelling of Marguerite, the French form of Margaret, from Greek margarites, pearl. In French marguerite is also the word for the daisy.
A shortened form of Virginia, from the Roman family name Verginius, long associated with Latin virgo, maiden.
A spelling of Edmond or Edmund, from Old English ead, wealth or fortune, and mund, protection. Saint Edmund was a 9th-century king of East Anglia.
A variant spelling of Reta, itself a form of Rita, the short form of Margarita, from Greek margarites, pearl.
An elaboration of Cleo, from Greek kleos, glory, with the -ola ending that was fashionable around 1900.
A short form of Washington, which Americans gave as a first name in honor of George Washington. The surname comes from a village in northeast England.
e.note: Identical to the everyday word wash.

e.etymology: A form of Ottilie and Odilia, feminine names built on the Germanic root od or aud, wealth. Saint Odilia is the patron of Alsace.
A spelling of Beulah, Hebrew for married. In Isaiah 62:4 it is a name promised to the land of Israel, and in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress the Land of Beulah lies at the edge of heaven.
Latin for chosen, taken from the elect lady addressed in the Second Epistle of John. Electa is one of the five heroines of the Order of the Eastern Star.
An English surname from several villages called Belton. Towns in Texas, Missouri and South Carolina carry the name too.
A contracted form of Adeline, the French pet form of Adele, from Germanic adal, noble.
A transposed spelling of Dwayne, from the Irish surname O Dubhain, descendant of Dubhan, a pet form of dubh, dark or black. It is best known from basketball star Dwyane Wade.
namesakes: Dwyane Wade (Hall of Fame guard who won three NBA titles with the Miami Heat)

e.etymology: A spelling of Orval, a form of Orville, the name Fanny Burney created for the hero of her 1778 novel Evelina. It looks French but has no known earlier history.
The French feminine form of Leontius, a late Roman name from Greek leon, lion. The soprano Leontyne Price bears a respelled form.
A 1970s spelling of Brandy, which Americans took up as a girls' name in the mid-20th century from the word for the spirit. Brandy is short for brandywine, from Dutch brandewijn, burnt wine.
An English and Scottish surname from an old Germanic personal name ending in berht, bright. A halbert is also a pole weapon, though the name is not taken from it.
A spelling of Gus, the short form of August and Augustus, Latin for venerable, and also of Gustav.
A spelling of the surname Buell used as a given name.
A pet form of Hester, the English variant of Esther.
Both a surname and the English word for a soft shine, used as a boys' name around 1900.
